title: Reading the Label
description: What a label must tell you, what it only implies and how quality systems differ between Europe and the rest of the world.
L: List the information most labels must show

Most wine labels must show the producer or bottler, the country of origin, the alcohol by volume, the volume of the bottle and allergen warnings. Wines with a geographical indication must name it. Since December 2023, EU labels must also give nutrition and ingredient information, often through a QR code.

The vintage is the year the grapes were picked. In the EU, if it is stated, at least 85% of the grapes must be from that year. Wines with over 10 mg/l of sulphur dioxide must say contains sulphites. Almost all wines do, since sulphur dioxide protects against oxygen and bacteria, and yeast makes a little naturally.
Vintage: at least 85% from that year in the EU
What does the vintage on a European label mean?
The year the wine was bottled
The year at least 85% of the grapes were harvested
The year the vineyard was planted
The year the wine was released
Vintage is the harvest year. In the EU, at least 85% of the grapes must come from the stated year.

Wines fined with egg or milk products must say so if any residue remains. Many vegans look for wines fined with bentonite clay or pea protein instead, or unfined wines. Some producers now state vegan on the label, but that term isn't regulated everywhere.
Egg and milk fining must be declared
A wine labelled contains sulphites has had unusually large amounts of chemicals added.
Not true. The warning applies above 10 mg/l, which covers almost every wine. Yeast produces some sulphur dioxide itself.
Labels must show producer, origin, abv, volume and allergens
In the EU, a stated vintage means at least 85% of grapes from that year
Contains sulphites applies to almost all wines
Explain what a geographical indication is
Explain why place names are protected

A geographical indication, or GI, is a legally defined area whose name can only be used by wines from there. Champagne, Rioja and Napa Valley are all GIs. Using the name promises origin, and often more: in Europe, rules may set grapes, yields and winemaking.
A GI is a protected place name

The EU has two levels. PDO, Protected Designation of Origin, is stricter: grapes must all come from the area, and rules cover varieties, yields, methods and ageing. PGI, Protected Geographical Indication, covers larger areas with looser rules: at least 85% of grapes from the area, and wider grape choices. Each country has its own names for them.
Match each term to its meaning.
Each step down the ladder gives producers more freedom and the consumer less information about place.

Place names became valuable, so others copied them. Before protection, sparkling wines worldwide called themselves Champagne. Today, EU agreements protect GIs in many countries. In the US, some older semi-generic names like California Champagne can still appear on bottles approved before 2006, but no new ones.
Protection stops others using famous names
What does PDO require that PGI does not?
All grapes from the defined area
PDO requires all grapes from the area and stricter rules. PGI requires at least 85%.
A GI is a legally protected place name
Protection stops famous names being copied
Name the national terms for PDO and PGI
Explain the extra tiers in Italy and Spain

Each EU country names its levels. France: AOC or AOP for PDO, IGP or Vin de Pays for PGI. Italy: DOCG and DOC for PDO, IGT for PGI. Spain: DOCa or DOQ and DO for PDO, Vino de la Tierra for PGI. Portugal: DOC for PDO, Vinho Regional for PGI.
AOC, DOC, DO: the PDO family

Italy's DOCG is a top tier, with stricter rules and tasting approval; Barolo and Chianti Classico are DOCG. Spain's DOCa, for Rioja and Priorat, works similarly. Germany's PDO wines are graded partly by sugar in the grapes at harvest: Qualitätswein, then Prädikatswein with six levels, from Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese.
DOCG and DOCa sit above DOC and DO
Match each term to its country.
Every EU country uses its own words for the same two levels, sometimes with extra tiers.

When a label from Europe names a region and nothing else, it's usually a PDO. Look up the rules once and you'll know the grape for life: Chablis is Chardonnay, Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc, Barolo is Nebbiolo.
Order Germany's Prädikat levels from least to most ripe.
Eiswein sits beside Beerenauslese in required ripeness, but is made from frozen grapes.
Each EU country has its own names for PDO and PGI
Italy's DOCG and Spain's DOCa are top tiers
Germany grades Prädikatswein by ripeness at harvest
Explain how New World labels work
Describe the AVA and GI systems

New World labels usually lead with the grape variety and the brand. GIs exist but generally only define the area; they don't set grapes, yields or methods. A Napa Valley wine can be any variety, made any way, as long as the grapes come from Napa.

Labelling rules set minimums. In the US, a varietal label needs 75% of the named grape, and an AVA name needs 85% of the grapes from that area. In Australia, Chile, New Zealand and South Africa, the figure is usually 85% for variety, vintage and region. A state or county name in the US needs 75%.
A Californian wine labelled Cabernet Sauvignon must contain at least how much of that grape?
US federal law requires 75% for a varietal label. Many other New World countries use 85%.

Terms like Reserve, Private Selection or Old Vines usually have no legal meaning in the New World. A few exceptions exist: in Washington, Reserve must be a small part of production, and South Africa's Wine of Origin seal certifies origin. Treat most extra words as marketing.
An AVA in the United States sets which grapes may be grown.
Not true. An AVA defines only the area. Growers can plant any grape and make wine as they choose.
New World labels lead with grape and brand
GIs define area, not style or grapes
Percentage rules set minimums for variety, vintage and region
Explain Spanish and Italian ageing terms
Recognise terms with no legal meaning

Some terms set minimum ageing. In Spain, Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva each require more time in oak and bottle; Rioja Gran Reserva reds need at least five years, with two in oak. In Italy, Riserva means longer ageing than the standard wine, with rules set for each DOC. Portugal's Reserva requires higher alcohol and quality approval.

Sparkling wines use a scale based on grams of sugar per litre: Brut Nature up to 3, Extra Brut up to 6, Brut up to 12, Extra Dry 12 to 17, Dry 17 to 32, Demi-Sec 32 to 50, Doux over 50. Still wines use terms like sec, demi-sec, moelleux and doux in France, or trocken and halbtrocken in Germany.
Which sparkling wine term means the driest of these?
Brut, up to 12 g/l, is drier than Extra Dry, 12 to 17 g/l. The naming is confusing but legal.

Many attractive words have no legal meaning in many countries: Reserve outside Europe, Old Vines, Natural and Premium. Organic, by contrast, is regulated: certified organic wine must follow rules on farming and winemaking, including lower sulphur limits in the EU.
Organic is regulated; Old Vines usually isn't
Which terms have a legal ageing meaning in Spain?
Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva are regulated. Old Vines has no legal definition.
Spanish and Italian terms like Reserva and Riserva set minimum ageing
Sparkling sweetness terms follow a sugar scale, with Brut dry
Many attractive words, like Old Vines, have no legal meaning
Interpret European and New World systems
In the EU, a stated vintage means at least what share of grapes from that year?
85% in the EU, and in many New World countries too.
Match each term to its country.
Every country has its own terms for protected places.
A PGI wine has stricter rules than a PDO wine.
Not true. PDO is stricter; PGI covers larger areas with looser rules.
Order these sparkling wine terms from driest to sweetest.
Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, which surprises many people.
Which of these are usually defined by law?
Gran Reserva and Organic are regulated. Old Vines and US Reserve generally aren't.
Labels must show producer, origin, abv, volume and allergens
PDO is stricter than PGI; each country names them differently
New World GIs define area only
Ageing and sweetness terms are regulated; many others are marketing
